div.p:
Children, Gracegrace be with you, Amen. I being taken from you in presence, and so tied up, that I cannot perform that duty, that from God doth
lie upon me, to you-wardyouward, for your further edifying and building up in Faithfaith and Holinessholiness, &etc.c., yetyetYet that you may see my Soulsoul hath fatherly care and desire after your spiritual and everlasting welfare,; I now once again, as beforebefore, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, so now from the Lionslions’ Densdens, and from the Mountainsmountains of the Leopardsleopards ((S. of Song 4.: 8.)), do look yet after you all, greatly longing to see your safe Arrivalarrival into THEthe desired Havenhaven.

I thank God upon every Remembranceremembrance of you,; and rejoicerejoice, even while I stick between the Teethteeth of the Lionslions in the Wildernesswilderness, at the Gracegrace, and Mercymercy, and Knowledgeknowledge of Christ our Saviour, which God hath bestowed upon you, with abundance of Faithfaith and Lovelove. Your Hungringshungerings and Thirstingsthirstings also after further Acquaintanceacquaintance with the Father, in hisHis Son; your Tendernesstenderness of Heartheart, your Tremblingtrembling at Sinsin, your sober and holy Deportmentdeportment alsoalso, before both God and Menmen, is great Refreshmentrefreshment to me; for‘For you are my Gloryglory and Joyjoy’, ( 1 Thes.Thess 2.: 2020).

I have sent you here inclosedenclosed, a drop of that Honeyhoney, that I have taken out of the Carcasecarcase of a Lionlion, ( Judg. 1414: 5, 6, 7, 8–9). I have eaten thereof my selfmyself also, and am much refreshed thereby. (Temptations, when we meet them at first, are as the Lionlion that roared upon SampsonSamson; but if we overcome them, the next time we see them, we shall find a Nestnest of Honeyhoney within them.) The Philistines understand me not. It is somethingsomething of a Relation. ofOfrelation of the Workwork of God upon my Soulsoul, even from the very first, till now; wherein you may perceive my Castingscastings down, and, Risings risings up; for he woundeth, and his hands make whole. It is written in the ScriptureScripture (Isa 38:19), Isa. 38. 19.‘ The father to the children shall make known the truth of God..’ Yea, it was for this Reasonreason I lay so long at Sinai, Lev. (Deut 4.: 10, 11.)), to see the Firefire, and the Cloudcloud, and the Darknessdarkness, that I might fear the Lord all the days of my Lifelife upon Earthearth, and tell of his wondrous Worksworks to my Childrenchildren, Psal(Ps. 78.: 3, 4,– 55).

Moses, Numb. (Num 33.: 1, 2.) writwritWrit of the Journeyingsjourneyings of the Childrenchildren of Israel, from Egypt, to the Landland of Canaan; and commanded also, that they did remember their forty Yearsyears’ Traveltravel in the Wilderness:wilderness. ‘ Thou shalt remember all the way which the Lord thy God led thee these forty years in the Wildernesswilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, and to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or nono’, ( Deut. 8.: 2, 3). Wherefore this I have endeavoured to do; and not only so, but to publish it also; that, if God will, others may be put in remembrance of what heHe hath done for their Soulssouls, by reading hisHis Workwork upon me.

It is profitable for Christians to be often calling to mind the very Beginningsbeginnings of Gracegrace with their Soulssouls.. ‘ It is a night to be much observed to the Lord, for bringing them out from the Landland of Egypt.: Thisthis is that Nightnight of the Lord, to be observed of all the Childrenchildren of Israel, in their Generationsgenerations’, ( ExodExod 12:42). 12. 42.‘ My God,,’ saith DavidDavid (Ps 42:6), Psal., 42. 6. My‘my Soulsoul
is cast down within me; but I will remember thee from the Landland of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the Hillhill Mizar..’ He remembredremembered also the Lionlion and the Bearbear, when he went to fight with the Giantgiant of Gath, ( 1 Sam. 17.: 36, 3737).

It was Paul’s accustomed mannermanner (Acts 22), Act. 22. andAndand that, when tried for his Lifelife (Acts 24), Act. 24. evenEveneven to openopen, before his Judgesjudges, the manner of his Conversionconversion: Hehe would think of that Dayday, audand that Hourhour, in which he first did meet with Gracegrace; for he found it supported him. When God had brought the Childrenchildren of Israel out of the Red -Sea, far into the Wildernesswilderness;, yet they must turn quite about thither again, to remember the drowning of their Enemiesenemies there, Numb. (Num 14.: 2525). forFor though they sang hisHis Praisepraise before, yetyet ‘ they soon forgat his Works, Psal.works’ (Ps 106.: 11, 12–13).

In this Discoursediscourse of mine, you may see much; much, I say, of the Gracegrace of God towards me:. I thank God, I can count it much;, for it was above my Sins,sins and Satan'sSatan’s Temptationstemptations too. I can remember my Fearsfears, and Doubtsdoubts, and sad
Monthsmonths with comfort; they are as the Headhead of GoliahGoliath in my Handhand:. There was nothing to David like Goliah’sGoliath’s Swordsword, even that Swordsword that should have been sheathed in his Bowelsbowels; for the very sight and remembrance of that did preach forth God’s Deliverancedeliverance to him. Oh, the Remembranceremembrance of my great Sinssins, of my great Temptationstemptations, and of my great Fearsfears of perishing for ever! They bring fresh into my Mindmind the Remembranceremembrance of my great Helphelp, my great Supportsupport from Heavenheaven, and the great Gracegrace that God extended to such a Wretchwretch as I.

My dear Childrenchildren, call to mind the former Daysdays, and Yearsyears of ancient Timestimes: Rememberremember also your Songssongs in the Nightnight,; and commune with your own Hearts, Psal. 73.hearts (Ps 77: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11,– 1212). Yea, look diligently, and leave no Cornercorner therein unsearched;, for thatthere is Treasuretreasure hid, even the Treasuretreasure of your first and second Experienceexperience of the Gracegrace of God toward you. Remember, I say, the Wordword that first laid hold upon you:; Rememberremember your Terrorsterrors of Conscienceconscience, and Fearfear of Deathdeath
and Hellhell:; Rememberremember also your Tearstears and Prayersprayers to God; yea, how you sighed under every Hedgehedge of Mercymercy. Have you never ana Hillhill Mizar to remember? Have you forgot the Closeclose, the Milk-milk house, the Stablestable, the Barnbarn, and the like, where God did visit your Soulssouls? Remember also the Word;— the Word, I say, upon which the Lord hath caused you to hope:. If you have sinned against Lightlight,; if you are tempted to blaspheme,; if you are down in Despairdespair,; if you think God fights against you,; or if Heavenheaven is hid from your Eyeseyes;, remember, it was thus with your Fatherfather;, but out of them all the Lord delivered me.

I could have enlarged much in this my Discoursediscourse, of my Temptationstemptations and Troublestroubles for Sinsin; as also, of the merciful Kindness,kindness and Workingworking of God with my Soulsoul:. I could also have stepped into a Stilestyle much higher than this, in which I have here discoursed, and could have adorned all things more than here I have seemed to do;, but I dare not:. GodGod did not play in convincing of me, the devil did not play in tempting of me;, neither did I play, when I sunk as
into a bottomless Pitpit, when the Pangspangs of Hellhell caught hold upon me; wherefore I may not play in relating of them, but be plain and simple, and lay down the thing as it was:. He that liketh it, let him receive it; and he that does not, let him produce a better. FarewelFarewell.
The the Milkmilk and Honeyhoney is beyond this Wildernesswilderness:, God be merciful to you, and grant you be not slothful to go in to possess the Landland.

div.head: Grace Abounding TO THE CHIEF OF SINNERS: OR, A brief Relation of the exceeding Mercy of God in Christ, to his poor Servant, John Bunyan.
div.p: IN1. In this my relation of the merciful working of God upon my Soulsoul, it will not be amiss, ifif, in the first place, I do, in a few words, give you ana hint of my Pedigreepedigree, and manner of bringing up; that thereby the goodness and bounty of God towards me, may be the more advanced and magnified before the sons of men.

2. For my Descentdescent then, it was, as is well known by many, of a low and inconsiderable generation; my father’s house being of that rank that is meanest, and most despised of all the families in the Landland. Wherefore I have not here, as others, to boast of Noblenoble Bloodblood, or of ana high-born statestate, according to the flesh; though, all things considered, I magnifiemagnify the heavenly Majesty, for that by this door heHe brought me into this Worldworld, to partake of the Gracegrace and Lifelife that is in Christ by the Gospelgospel.

3. But yet, notwithstanding the meanness and inconsiderableness of my Parentsparents, it pleased God to put it into their hearts, to put me to Schoolschool, to learn both to read and write; the which I also attained, according to the rate of other poor Mensmen’s children; thoughthough, to my shame, I confess, I did soon lose that little I learntlearned, even almost utterly, and that long before the Lord did work hisHis gracious work of Conversionconversion upon my Soulsoul.

4. As for my own natural life, for the time that I was without God in the world, it was, indeed, according to the course of this world, andand ‘ the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobediencedisobedience’, ( Eph. 2.: 2, 33). It was my delight, to bebe ‘ taken captive by the Devil,devil at his willwill’, ( 2 Tim. 22: 2626). beingBeing filled with all unrighteousness The, the which did also so strongly work,
and put forth it selfitself, both in my heart and life, and that from a child, that I had but few Equalsequals (, especially considering my years, which were tender, being few), both for cursing, swearing, lyinglying, and blaspheming the holy Namename of God.

5. Yea, so setledsettled and rooted was I in these things, that they became as a second Naturenature to me; the which, as I also have with soberness considered since, did so offend the Lord, that even in my childhood heHe did scare and affright me with fearful dreams, and did terrifieterrify me with dreadful visions:; Forfor often, after I had spent this and the other day in sin, I have in my bed been greatly afflicted, while asleep, with the apprehensions of Devils,devils and wicked Spiritsspirits, who still, as I then thought, laboured to draw me away with them;, of which I could never be rid.

6. Also I should, at these years, be greatly afflicted and troubled with the thoughts of thethe day of judgment, and that both night and day, and should tremble at the thoughts of the fearful torments of Hell-hell fire; still fearing that it would be my lot to be found, at last, among those Devils,devils and hellish Fiendsfiends, who are there bound down with the chains and bonds of darkness,, ‘ unto the judgment of the great Dayday..’

7. These things, I say, when I was but a child, about nine or ten years old, did so distress my Soulsoul, that then, in the midst of my
many Sports,sports and childish vanities, amidst my vain companions, I was often much cast down and afflicted in my mind therewith;, yet could I not let go my sins:. Yea, I was also then so overcome with despair of Lifelife and Heavenheaven, that I should often wish, either that there had been no Hellhell, or that I had been a Devildevil;— supposing they were only tormentors,; that if it must needs be, that I indeed went thither, I might be rather a tormentor, than be tormented my selfmyself.

8. A while after, these terrible dreams did leave me, which I also soon forgot; for my pleasures did quickly cut off the remembrance of them, as if they had never been: Whereforewherefore, with more greediness, according to the strength of nature, I did still let loose the reins to my lust, and delighted in all transgression against the Lawlaw of God: Soso thatthat, until I came to the state of Marriagemarriage, I was the very ringleader of all the Youthyouth that kept me company, in all manner of vice and ungodliness.

9. Yea, such prevalency had the lusts and fruits of the flesh, in this poor Soulsoul of mine, that had not a miracle of precious Gracegrace prevented, I had not only perished by the stroakstroke of Eternaleternal Justicejustice, but had also laid my selfmyself open, even to the stroakstroke of those Lawslaws, which bring some to disgrace, and open shame, before the face of the world.

10. In these daysdays, the thoughts of Religionreligion were very grievous to me; I could neither endure it my selfmyself, nor that any other should:; Soso thatthat, when I have seen some read in these books that concerned Christian Pietypiety, it would be as it were a prison to me. Then I said unto God,, ‘ Depart from me, for I desire not the knowledge of thy waysways’, ( Job 21.: 14, 15). I was now void of all good consideration;, Heavenheaven and Hellhell were both out of sight and mind; and as for Savingsaving and Damningdamning, they were least in my thoughts. O Lord, thouThou knowest my life;, and my ways were not hid from theeThee.

11. But this I well remember, Thatthat though I could my selfmyself sin with the greatest delight and Easeease, and also take pleasure in the vileness of my companions; yetyet, even then, if I have at any time seen wicked thingsthings, by those who professed goodness, it would make my spirit tremble. As once, above all the rest, when I was in my height of vanity, yet hearing one to swear, that was reckoned for a religious man, it had so great a stroakstroke upon my spirit, that it made my heart akeache.

12. But God did not utterly leave me, but followed me still;, not now with convictions, but judgments; yetyet, such as were mixed with mercy. For once I fell into a crickcreek of the Seasea, and hardly escaped drowning:. Another time I fell out of a Boat,boat into Bedford-River river,
but Mercymercy yet preserved me alive:. Besides, another time, being in the field with one of my companions, it chanced that an Adderadder passed over the high-wayhighway; so II, having a stick in minemy hand, struck her over the back; and having stunned her, I forced open her mouth with my stick, and plucked her sting out with my fingers;, by which act, had not God been merciful to me, I might, by my desperateness, have brought my selfmyself to mine end.

13. This also I have taken notice of, with thanksgiving; Whenwhen I was a Soldiersoldier, I, with others, were drawn out to go to such a place to besiege it; but when I was just ready to go, one of the Companycompany desired to go in my room; to which, when I had consented, he took my place; and coming to the Siegesiege, as he stood Sentinelsentinel, he was shot into the head with a Musket-musket bullet, and died.

14. Here, as I said, were Judgmentsjudgments and Mercymercy, but neither of them did awaken my Soulsoul to Righteousnessrighteousness; wherefore I sinned still, and grew more and more rebellious against God, and careless of mine own Salvationsalvation.

15. Presently after this, I changed my condition into a married state;, and my mercy was, to light upon a wife, whose father was counted godly:. This woman and I, though we came together as poor as poor might be, (not having so much house-hold-household stuff as a dish
or spoon betwixt us both), yet this she had for her part, The Plain Man’s Path-wayPathway to Heaven, and The Practice of Piety, which her father had left her, when he died. In these two books I should sometimes read with her, wherein I also found some things that were somewhat pleasing to me; (but all this while I met with no conviction.) She also would be often telling of me, what a godly man her father was, and how he would reprove and correct vice, both in his house, audand amongst his neighbours; what a strict and holy life he lived in his day, both in Wordword and deed.

16. Wherefore these books, with this Relationrelation, though they did not reach my heart, to awaken it about my sad and sinful state, yet they did beget within me some desires to Religionreligion: Soso that, because I knew no better, I fell in very eagerly with the Religionreligion of the times; to wit, to go to Churchchurch twice a day, and that too with the foremost; and there should very devoutly, both say and sing as others did, yet retaining my wicked life:; Butbut withal, I was so over-runoverrun with the spirit of Superstitionsuperstition, that I adored, and that with great devotion, even all things (, both the High-high place, Priestpriest, Clerkclerk, vestments, Serviceservice, and what else) belonging to the Churchchurch; counting all things holy, that were therein contained;, and especially, the Priestpriest and Clerkclerk most happy, and without
doubtdoubt, greatly blessed, because they were the Servantsservants, as I then thought, of God;, and were principal in the holy Templetemple, to do hisHis work therein.

17. This conceit grew so strong, in little time, upon my spirit, that had I but seen a Priestpriest (, though never so sordid and debauched in his life), I should find my spirit fall under him, reverence him, and knit unto himhim: yea, I thought, for the love I did bear unto them (, supposing they were the Ministersministers of God), I could have lain down at their feetfeet, and have been trampled upon by them; their Namename, their Garbgarb, and Workwork, did so intoxicate and bewitch me.

18. After I had been thus for some considerable time, another thought came in my mind; and that was, Whetherwhether we were of the Israelites, or no? For finding in the Scriptures that they were once the peculiar people of God, thought I, Ifif I were once of this racerace, my Soulsoul must needs be happy. Now againagain, I found within me a great longing to be resolved about this Questionquestion, but could not tell how I should:. At last, I asked my father of it; who told me,,— No, we were not. Where foreWherefore then I fell in my spirit, as to the hopes of that, and so remained.

19. But all this while, I was not sensible of the danger and evil of sin; I was kept from
considering that sin would damn me, what Religionreligion soever I followed, unless I was found in Christ:. Nay, I never thought of himHim, nor whether there was such ana one, or nono. Thus Manman, while blind, doth wander, but wearieth himself with vanity., forforFor he knoweth not the way to the Citycity of God, Eccles. (Eccl 10.: 1515).

20. But one day (, amongst all the Sermonssermons our Parsonparson made), his Subjectsubject was, to treat of the Sabbath-day, and of the evil of breaking that, either with labour, sports, or otherwise:. Now I was, notwithstanding my Religionreligion, one that took much delight in all manner of vice;, and especially, that was the day that I did solace my selfmyself therewith.) Wherefore, wherefore I fell in my Conscienceconscience under his Sermonsermon, thinking and believing that he made that Sermonsermon on purpose to shewshow me my evil -doing:; Andand at that time I felt what guilt was, though never before, that I can remember; but then iI was, for the present, greatly loaden therewith, and so went home when the Sermonsermon was ended, with a great burthenburden on my spirit.

21. This, for that instant, did benumb the sinews of my best delights, and did imbitter my former pleasures to me:; Butbut behold, it lasted not;, for before I had well dined, the trouble began to go off my Mindmind, and my heart returned to it'sits old course: Butbut Ohoh! how glad was I, that this trouble was gone
from me, and that the fire was put out, that I might sin again without control! WhereforeWherefore, when I had satisfied Naturenature with my food, I shook the Sermonsermon out of my mind, and to my old custom of sports and gaming I returned with great delight.

22. But the same day, as I was in the midst of a game at Catcat, and having struck it one blow from the hole, just as I was about to strike it the second time, a voice did suddenly dart from Heaven,heaven into my Soulsoul, which said,, “ Wilt thou leave thy sins, and go to Heavenheaven;, or have thy sins, and go to Hellhell??” At this I was put to an exceeding maze; wherefore, leaving my Catcat upon the ground, I looked up to Heavenheaven, and was as if I had, with the eyes of my understanding, seen the Lord Jesus looking down upon me, as being very hotly displeased with me, and as if heHe did severely threaten me with some grievous punishment for these, and other my ungodly practices.

23. I had no sooner thus conceived in my mind, but suddainlysuddenly this conclusion was fastened on my spirit (, for the former hint did set my sins again before my face:), Thatthat I had been a great and grievous sinner, and that it was now too late for me to look after Heavenheaven; for Christ would not forgive me, nor pardon my transgressions. Then I fell to musing upon this alall soalso; and while I was thinking of it, and fearing
lest it should be so, I felt my heart sink in despair, concluding it was too late; and therefore I resolved in my mind, I would go on in sin:; Forfor, thought I, if the case be thus, my state is surely miserable; miserable if I leave my sins, and but miserable if I follow them:; I can but be damned;, and if it must be so, I had as good be damned for many sins, as be damned for few.

24. Thus I stood in the midst of my play, before all that then were present; but yet I told them nothing: But,but I say, I having made this conclusion, I returned desperately to my sport again; and I well remember, that presently this kind of despair did so possess my Soulsoul, that I was perswadedpersuaded, I could never attain to other comfort than what I should get in sin; for Heavenheaven was gone already, so that on that I must not think:; Whereforewherefore I found within me a great desire to take my fill of sin, still studying what sin was yet to be committed, that I might taste the sweetness of it; and I made as much haste as I could to fill my belly with its delicates, lest I should die before I had my desire; for that I feared greatly. In these things, I protest before God, I lyelie not, neither do I feign this form of speech; these were really, strongly, and with all my heart, my desires:; Thethe good LordLord, whose mercy is unsearchable, forgive me my transgressions.

25. (And I am very confident, that this temptation of the Devildevil is more usual amongst poor creatures than many are aware of, even to over-runoverrun the spirits with a scurfyscurvy and seared frame of heart, and benumbing of conscience; which frameframe, he stilly and slily supplieth with such despair, that though not much guilt attendeth Soulssouls, yet they continually have a secret conclusion within them, that there is no hopes for them; for they have loved sins,, ‘ therefore after them they will gogo’, ( JerJer 2:25; 18:12). 2 25. andAnd 18. 12.)

26. Now therefore I went on in sin with great greediness of mind, still grudging that I could not be so satisfied with it as I would. This did continvecontinue with me about a monthmonth, or more:; Butbut one day, as I was standing at a neighbour’s shop-window, and there cursing and swearing, and playing the mad-manmadman, after my wonted manner, there sat within the woman of the house, and heard me;, who, though she also was a very loose and ungodly wretch, yet protested that I swore and cursed at that most fearful rate, that she was made to tremble to hear me; and told me further, Thatthat I was the ungodliest fellow, for swearing, that ever she heard in all her life; and that I, by thus doing, was able to spoil all the Youthyouth in the whole Towntown, if they came but in my company.

27. At this reproof I was silenced, and put to secret shame;, and that too., asasAs I thought, before the God of Heaven: Whereforeheaven; wherefore, while I stood there, and hanging down my head, I wished with all my heart that I might be a little child again, that my father might learn me to speak without this wicked way of swearing; for, thought I, I am so accustomed to it, that it is but in vain for me to think of a reformation, for I thought it could never bebe.

28. But how it came to pass, I know not; I did, from this time forward, so leave my swearing, that it was a great wonder to my selfmyself to observe it; and whereas before I knew not how to speak, unless I put an Oathoath before, and another behind, to make my words have authority;, now I could, without it, speak better, and with more pleasantness, than ever I could before. All this while I knew not Jesus Christ, neither did I leave my sports and play.

29. But quickly after this, I fell in company with one poor man, that made profession of Religionreligion; who, as I then thought, did talk pleasantly of the Scriptures, and of the matters of Religion: Whereforereligion; wherefore, falling into some love and liking to what he saidsaid, I betook me to my Bible, and began to take great pleasure in reading, but especially with the Historicalhistorical part thereof; forfor, as for Paul’s Epistlesepistles, and such likesuchlike Scriptures, I could not
away with them;, being as yet ignorant, either of the corruptions of my nature, or of the want and worth of Jesus Christ to save me.
